3 tips for getting the best deals this holiday shopping season
Economy
Nov 25, 2026 4:19 PM EST
Holiday shopping season is officially here, and the National Retail Federation forecasts that this year's sales could top a record $1 trillion, even as many Americans report feeling the pain of rising prices and inflation.
READ MORE: The holiday season can be expensive. Here are some tips for keeping credit card debt in check
"Despite the fact that Americans are struggling to make ends meet, they are not willing to give up the holiday season," said Andrea Woroch, a consumer saving and spending expert.
Online holiday sales will hit $275 billion, according to Adobe's holiday sales forecast, which also predicts a record 63% of sales will happen on mobile devices. And a new trend is emerging, says Adobe's lead insight analyst Vivek Pandya: using Cyber Week to stock up on everyday essentials. Personal hygiene product sales are expected to jump 150% this year, Adobe's data shows.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
With the ever-changing landscape of holiday shopping, how do you know you're getting the best deal?
WATCH: What's driving up the cost of Thanksgiving dinner
Woroch and Pandya offered these three tips.
1. Black Friday and Cyber Monday are still the best times to get deep discounts, but not for every item on your list
This year, "we won't see as wide a selection of doorbusters like we have in the past," Woroch said.
WATCH: Shopping for holiday gifts online? Here are tips for avoiding scams
What are some of the best deals to find on Black Friday? "Products that have plugs, so small personal gadgets, small kitchen appliances, smart home devices, even beauty tools like blow dryers, and then household cleaning products like vacuums," she said.
Deep discounts on electronics and apparel peak during Cyber Week, but this year, so will sales on everyday items.
Consumers will "see these different types of categories being marked down, especially personal care products, cosmetics, and they're really using these moments as an opportunity to stock up for the year ahead."
2. The best way to avoid overspending during cyber week? Make a plan
To stay on track, Woroch says, list the people you need to buy for and specific gift ideas. Then, set a realistic budget that doesn't rely on credit cards or taking cash from essential bills.
This guide means "you're not shopping aimlessly and then leading to impulse purchases or overbuying. So that's gonna be a really important tool as you approach sales events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday."
You can also research current prices and historical pricing data from the last six months before the big shopping days arrive.
"See what things cost before the deal drops. This will just give you better information to make better buying decisions so that you can spot the really good deals when they do become available."
Woroch also has a pretty reliable rule of thumb: If something you've been searching for is 30% off, you should buy it.
"Chances are it's not going to get much cheaper than that."
3. Love it or hate it, AI can help you find the best deal
Pandya expects traffic from AI platforms to retail sites to be up 140% from last year.
This is in part because AI-powered chat and browser services can supercharge your hunt for deals.
READ MORE: Your guide to holiday gifting when money is tight
Not sure where to start? Woroch suggests entering a product name, along with some prompts like "compare prices across every retailer selling this item, apply any working coupon codes or free shipping offers to get me the lowest possible deal."
You can also ask: "Can you find me a cheaper option for a similar item?"
These strategies helped Woroch save $20 on a gift from her own list this year.
"Imagine you multiply that across all the gifts on your list, that can add up to big savings."

Protesters take to the streets in Puerto Rico's capital as standard of living deteriorates
Nation
Nov 27, 2026 5:10 PM EST
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — Thousands of people protested Friday in Puerto Rico's capital as anger and frustration erupted over record high electric rates, the surging cost of living, deterioration in basic services and other issues.
Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined the protest organized by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organizations. The crowds gathered in front of the largest mall in the Caribbean on Black Friday for what organizers dubbed the "Day of National Outrage."
Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island.
WATCH: Drought and aging infrastructure plunge Puerto Rico into a water crisis
Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radamés García Badillo said "Where to start? The outrage is absolute."
He noted that power and water services are unreliable, with his neighborhood going dark at least once a week for several hours.
He also decried a sharp increase in the cost of living.
"We're buying less because things are extremely expensive," he said. "For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch."
The protest is one of the largest in the U.S. territory since Gov. Jenniffer González took office in January 2025, and it grew throughout the day as demonstrators took over one of the island's main highways, forcing its closure.
"Things have never been good in Puerto Rico, but they keep getting worse," said Verónica Ishtar, a 22-year-old visual arts student who drew sketches of the protesters.
This week alone, the power in her neighborhood went out 12 times, and she struggles to pay her power bill.
"This is not normal, and it should not be normalized," she said.
A firefighter wears a helmet with a Puerto Rican flag and a message on the visor calling for a dignified retirement during the "Day of National Indignation" protest in San Juan, Puerto Rico, on Nov. 27, 2026. Photo by Ricardo Arduengo/Reuters
Monthly electricity bills for some residential customers recently rose about 18%, from $229 to $271.
The new rate of 33.86 cents per kWh far surpasses the average rate of 18.3 cents per kWh for residential customers in the U.S. mainland, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Some protesters condemned Luma Energy, a private company that oversees the transmission and distribution of power on the island.
On Wednesday, Puerto Rico's Supreme Court narrowly approved canceling the government's contract with Luma. The governor praised the ruling, but many now worry about what comes next as outages persist.
Puerto Rico's Association of Industries said that the cancelation could "discourage private investment and jeopardize the continuity of projects in progress" as crews continue to repair a grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017 that was already weakened by a lack of maintenance and investment.
As the protest grew, one demonstrator pledged a "combative Christmas."
The leaders of several groups that organized the protest pledged to keep pushing for change.
"We must begin to channel the rage," said Hernaliz Vázquez, executive director of Sierra Club Puerto Rico. "We must begin to organize the indignation felt by people who do not know what to do."
Eva Prados, a politician, attorney and human rights advocate, was among the protesters.
She noted that power bills are unsustainable and businesses are closing as Puerto Ricans struggle with a high cost of living and basic services "that this government is not guaranteeing."
Puerto Rico "is awaiting concrete solutions," she said.

Mexico's government is slamming a DEA crime tip line as foreign interference. Others are thrilled.
World
Nov 27, 2026 4:36 PM EST
MEXICO CITY (AP) — The government in Mexico is railing against the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency's anonymous tip line for reports against criminals and corrupt officials in the Latin American nation, slamming it as foreign interference.
Others in Mexico are embracing it.
In the state of Sinaloa, journalist Juan Manuel Partida Valdez was among the first to write to the WhatsApp line on Thursday, just a day after DEA chief Terry Cole called for anonymous reports on his X account.
READ MORE: Mexico's most powerful cartels adapt as arrests and leadership battles reshape their ranks
The announcement opened the latest chapter in an ongoing struggle between the U.S. and Mexican governments over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico.
Partida Valdez, president of the Sinaloa Journalists Association, said he sent information about alleged ties between Sinaloa politicians and criminal groups because authorities have failed to put an end to violence and corruption that has bled his northern Mexican region dry in recent years.
He got a quick response, he said.
"I talk to so many people — in the streets, on social media, on WhatsApp and in chats — and you realize what people think: We're all fed up," the 67-year-old told The Associated Press on Friday. "We're fed up with narco-governments."
Mexico files a complaint against the tip line
On Friday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she escalated her fight with Washington over the tip line, filing a formal complaint with the U.S. Embassy for interfering in Mexico's internal affairs.
"We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," Sheinbaum said in her morning press briefing.
Sheinbaum once again urged Washington to address drug use and combat drug traffickers within its own territory while affirming that Mexico would continue working to confront cartels and prevent drugs from reaching the U.S.
READ MORE: Mexico detains top cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro,' setting off a burst of violence in Sinaloa
As U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Sheinbaum to crack down on criminal groups, Sheinbaum has underscored Mexican sovereignty at the same time her government has cracked down on cartels more forcefully than her predecessors.
Homicide rates have taken a sharp dip in Mexico and the government has taken out a number of top cartel bosses, often using U.S. intelligence to do so. The latest came over the weekend, when Mexican forces captured an important ally of a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, and requested that a U.S. surveillance drone fly over Mexican territory to help them pinpoint the location of the capo.
Criminals 'are being protected in our country'
At the same time, a number of scandals have soured that relationship.
In April, two CIA agents died following a drug lab bust with local authorities in northern Chihuahua.
Sheinbaum said her government was not informed that two U.S. intelligence agents were carrying out an operation in Mexican territory, paving the way for a potential treason trial.
Weeks later, Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — a powerful figure in Sheinbaum's party — was forced to step down after he was indicted by the U.S. on drug-trafficking charges in another political blow.
It was this case that Partida Valdez, the journalist, cited as a key reason for why he decided to reach out to the tip line, saying it was a "very clear example of what we're suffering because of these governments that do absolutely nothing but protect criminals."
"This whole song and dance about sovereignty is just collusion with the politicians tied to drug trafficking who are being protected in our country," he added.
WATCH: Mexico's foreign secretary on Trump, cartel violence and U.S. trade talks
While a number of observers warned of the dangers of the strategy by the DEA, other academics and politicians celebrated the line as a potential tool or said they trusted the intelligence agency more than their own government.
Lilly Téllez, a senator for Mexico's National Action Party, a weakened opposition party that has also been plagued by a number of corruption scandals, said she welcomed the tip line.
Téllez, a politician from the U.S.-Mexico border state of Sonora, wrote on X on Friday that the tip line is "a good way to cooperate against the common enemy of both countries" and strengthens efforts to combat cartels.
"On behalf of millions of Mexicans oppressed by the cartels, I ask President (Sheinbaum) not to obstruct the opportunity to gather more information to locate criminals and identify their activities," she wrote.
Associated Press journalist Megan Janetsky contributed to this report from Mexico City.

Canada's Supreme Court largely upholds a Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
World
Nov 27, 2026 3:48 PM EST
TORONTO (AP) — Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld most of a Quebec law banning public schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work. The ruling affirmed Quebec's power to override certain constitutional rights to keep the ban in place.
The 2019 law, known as Bill 21, bans religious symbols — including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses — for workers covered by it.
Canada has long embraced multiculturalism, encouraging people to retain their cultural and religious identities. Supporters of Quebec's ban say public officials should avoid wearing religious symbols to demonstrate government neutrality.
READ MORE: Pentagon sharply criticizes Canada over modernizing military
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon welcomed the ruling as "a victory for secularism" and for Quebec's ability to make different choices from the rest of Canada.
The court upheld Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause," which allows lawmakers to override certain rights, including religious freedom and equality. Those rights are protected by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Canada's equivalent of the U.S. Bill of Rights. Lawmakers must renew the override every five years to keep it in effect.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said he respected the ruling but pledged that his government would not use the constitutional override. He stressed that constitutional rights are particularly important for minorities and vulnerable people.
"Canada is a mosaic," Carney said, adding that it represents more than different backgrounds and identities. "It's a commitment, in my judgment, a commitment to how we treat each other."
Carney also welcomed the court's finding that judges can still declare that a law violates constitutional rights even when the override allows it to remain in force. He said that scrutiny helps inform Canadians and is useful in a democracy.
Chief Justice Richard Wagner wrote that the law reflected Quebec's "legitimate and historical commitment" to keeping government secular.
READ MORE: China and Canada expand tariff relief while relations with the U.S. are strained
The court maintained an exemption allowing members of Quebec's legislature to cover their heads — or potentially, for women, to cover their faces — while performing their duties.
Quebec's commitment to secularism grew from its rejection of the Roman Catholic Church's once-dominant influence.
Opponents say the law discriminates against religious minorities, particularly Muslim women who wear headscarves.
"Quebec is still telling qualified people that they must set aside their faith," said Mehramat Kaur of the World Sikh Organization of Canada.
France, Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands have full or partial bans on face coverings, including veils worn by some Muslim women.
Other Canadian provinces have used the override for laws restricting transgender rights or ordering striking employees back to work.
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew called Bill 21 "legislated discrimination" against Muslims, Sikhs and other religious minorities. He said his government would never use the override.
"If I need to pick on somebody in order to get elected, I don't deserve the office," Kinew said.

Army deems lead azide detonation a success but criticism lingers over notification
Nation
Nov 27, 2026 3:25 PM EST
The detonation of the nation's aging stockpile of lead azide, which spurred widespread concerns about potential environmental contamination, has been deemed a success by the U.S. Army. But questions remain about how and when the federal government communicated its plans.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said about 300 people spent Thursday in the field sampling schools, playgrounds, churches and homes across the region. Results were expected in the coming days.
More than 1,500 samples were taken of air, water, soil and dust before the detonation. After, they took hundreds of samples including from homes, parks and drinking water, the EPA has said.
WATCH: What the Army's Iowa detonation means for nearby communities
So far, the EPA said there has continued to be "zero" airborne lead detected in the region since Wednesday's controlled detonation.
While that's reassuring, residents and some elected officials have criticized the Army for not being more transparent and providing more notice when it first determined the stockpile was unstable.
A notice that plant managers planned to neutralize the stockpile was posted on a government website. Growing concern led to a plant closure in March that was publicized, and an October public meeting warned that the chemicals would soon need to be detonated.
Residents in the tiny town of Middletown, where the Army stockpile was held, knew of the plans, but few others did — and the warnings largely failed to register with elected officials and the broader public until days before the planned detonation.
Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand is among those calling for an investigation into why the lead azide was allowed to get to this precarious point.
"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," he said after the detonation.
Pause at the ammunition plant brings first notice to Middletown
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson and fellow residents said they were anything but blindsided. They learned of the problem when the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant was temporarily closed in March.
Johnson said he was briefed by the plant commander at the time and shown photos of the bunkers where the 68 barrels had been stored since being transferred there nearly two decades ago.
A working group assembled by the Army in January spent months charting a path forward and in October, about 200 residents attended a public meeting where experts outlined the urgency of detonating the hazardous material before it could spark a chain reaction of unintended explosions.
READ MORE: What is lead azide? What to know about the chemical detonated at an Iowa Army base
The Army said then they were aiming for a date in November and that the weather would dictate the schedule.
The Army submitted an application to the EPA in late October, winning approval from regulators within about two weeks. The lengthy document covered everything from the alternatives that had been considered to the environmental sampling that would follow and community engagement that was required.
"Because this action may raise public concerns related to noise, blast effects, and potential environmental contamination, this Community Engagement Plan establishes the framework for proactive, transparent communication with the EPA, local elected officials, the Middletown community, the media, and other interested stakeholders," the application states.
Critics blast the Army for not sharing info more widely
Johnson has said he believes the Army did its job.
"Unfortunately negative social media and unconfirmed theories have made this task more complicated for all parties involved," he said in a social media post after a legal challenge delayed the original Nov. 20 date for the detonation.
At the time, he said Middletown residents were fearful, not knowing when the lead azide would be taken care of so they could get on with their lives.
Environmentalists and other critics argued that the Army should have cast a wider net, providing information sooner to more downwind communities. They said contamination from toxic lead dust can have long-lasting health and environmental impacts and people needed time to prepare.
"The failure of communication and transparency throughout the planning process is inexcusable and left many Iowans feeling confused, helpless, and scared," said Josh Turek, a Democratic state lawmaker who was recently elected to Iowa's open U.S. Senate seat.
Public advisories for permits went unnoticed by many
The EPA issued public advisories about the flurry of required permitting as early as May. The agency said in a letter to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds that those notices went to Iowa's congressional delegation, state lawmakers and local officials.
Reynolds' office did not answer emails asking whether the governor knew about the plant's shutdown in March or the permit advisories. Some Democratic state lawmakers said they were blindsided, while Iowa House Majority Leader Bobby Kaufmann, a Republican, said he had concerns about how notification was handled.

U.S. military says it disabled another ship that tried to breach naval blockade on Iranian ports
World
Updated on Nov 27, 2026 4:10 PM EST — Published on
Nov 27, 2026 2:39 PM EST
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military has disabled a merchant ship in the Gulf of Oman that was trying to run its blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said Friday.
A military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," it said in a statement.
According to U.S. Central Command, the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel's destination as Singapore.
WATCH: 'We will not allow that to happen,' Trump says of reported Iran dirty bomb threat
The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations "that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region's waters."
The strike comes as the Trump administration weighs its options in the long-simmering war with Iran, which began at the end of February and has settled into a quiet stalemate in the past several months.
Earlier in November, officials in the region told The Associated Press that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the U.S. to restart the war or allow Israel to launch airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities and missile capabilities.
Meanwhile, government and security officials from the Persian Gulf countries, as well as Pakistan and Turkey, were engaged in a diplomatic campaign, which included phone calls with senior U.S. officials, to stave off a renewed war in the region.
President Donald Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the war "militarily is effectively over."
The U.S. military has maintained a sizable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.
The U.S. has been blockading Iranian ports since April, though the blockade was lifted in the summer during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the U.S. military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabling those that refuse to comply.
The Pacific Archer is at least the 15th disclosed vessel to be disabled by the U.S. military since the blockade began in the spring and the sixth since it resumed this summer. The previous vessel was disabled on Nov. 7.
In June, the practice drew condemnation when a military strike on a Guinea-Bissau-flagged tanker attempting to evade the American blockade resulted in three deaths.
READ MORE: Iran war has permanently reshaped energy priorities, IEA report says
Three Indian sailors were killed when American forces struck the Palau-flagged M/T Settebello, officials in India said at the time. The leader of the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency, condemned the attack.
U.S. Central Command has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.
The claims could not be independently verified.
In a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster, the country's Revolutionary Guard also said the number of oil tankers attempting to transit through unauthorized routes in the critical waterway has sharply decreased in recent days.
Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without approval from Tehran.
Oil flows in the first two weeks of November fell by around 20% to around 13 million barrels per day compared with October, when exports roughly equaled the prewar amounts of 15-16 million barrels per day, according to Rystad Energy.
Reasons for the November decline include Iranian attacks that discourage tankers from attempting the strait crossing and reduced flows through a key Saudi pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has also been attacked several times.
A report by U.N. Trade and Development finds that disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal are lengthening voyages, raising fuel costs, driving port congestion and adding to uncertainty. Alternative ports, inland transport and logistics arrangements have kept trade moving, but at a higher cost.
Toqa Ezzidin in Cairo contributed.

Using a drone and a poop-sniffing dog, scientists perform health checks on endangered orcas
Science
Updated on Nov 27, 2026 3:10 PM EST — Published on
Nov 27, 2026 1:43 PM EST
KINGSTON, Wash. (AP) — Every fall for the last few years, Deborah Giles starts her work day with one question in mind: Where are the orcas?
Giles is tracking the Southern Resident killer whales, an endangered species whose population recovery is faltering despite years of protection. In their search for their dwindling food source, the whales are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia. But in the last half-decade, the orcas have been hunting coho and chum salmon just north of Seattle during the fall.
Grow your mind
Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the
wide worlds of science, health and technology.
It's providing an opportunity for collaboration between The SeaDoc Society and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. They're using drones mounted with petri dishes and microscope slides to collect droplets from whale spouts and employing a poop-sniffing dog to find stool samples, providing much-needed wellness checks for as many of the 76 remaining whales as they can find.
"They were here before us, long before us," said Giles. "They're a group of animals that are uniquely bonded to this place and to each other."
Shrinking food source, disappearing whales
A research drone flown by Dr. James Sheppard of the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance hovers over K33 "Tika," a Southern Resident killer whale, while attempting to collect breath samples, on Puget Sound near Possession Point State Park, Washington, on Nov. 18, 2026. Photo by Lindsey Wasson/AP (NMFS/NOAA permit #26288-01)
Before colonization of the Pacific Northwest, the orca's main prey — Chinook salmon — could weigh more than 100 pounds (45.36 kilograms) and their numbers were abundant along the West Coast, Giles said.
But when American settlers came to the region, they built dams and overfished salmon. As cities and ports grew, boats created more noise, hindering the orca's hunting. Toxic chemicals flowed into sea water. And Chinook salmon now average about 12.5 pounds (5.66 kilograms), Giles said.
READ MORE: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
"We have completely changed their ability to live out their daily lives," Giles said.
The lack of fish has pushed the whales to hunt in the open ocean, where collecting research samples is difficult. The whales used to reliably spend their summers around the San Juan Islands, where Giles is based. No more. She moves her 22-foot (6.7-meter) boat further south in the fall in hopes of the opportunity to collect samples.
A chase by sea and air
The team crams into the small boat and motors fast to where Giles' contacts have reported sightings. With the orcas in view, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance drone pilot and senior scientist James Sheppard launches the drone from the boat's bow.
He hovers high first to hone in on a whale's location, then drops to just a dozen or so feet above the surface. He focuses on an adult male with a massive dorsal fin punching through the water. The spout spray reaches about 6 to 10 feet (1.8 to 3 meters) into the air, and it's as wide as a basketball, Sheppard said. As the whale breathes, the drone sweeps horizontally across the falling droplets.
"Once we've got the sample it's important we bring the drone back to the boat as quickly as possible so that the samples don't get degraded with the wind and the sunlight," Sheppard said.
WATCH: Scientists track humpback whale migration with an assist from AI technology
The conditions on this November day prove difficult. With less sunlight, the whales are harder to see, and they're foraging and surfacing unpredictably. They pay little mind to the drone, which is also equipped with cameras to record video and infrared sensors to capture a whale's body temperature.
"The few times that they've actually noticed the drone they'll just roll on their side, maybe look at it for a few seconds, and then just keep on swimming. To them, it's just a strange seagull that's been following them for a few seconds," said Sheppard, who recently won an award for his piloting and research.
After the drone, it's Eba's turn. The 11-year-old dog heads straight to the bow and sniffs the air, her head sticking out beyond the boat. She's held on a leash by Jim Rappold, Giles' husband and research partner. Eba picks up a scent, lets out a few whines and paces on the bow to alert her finding. But on this day, her human handlers couldn't find the feces she smelled.
Samples provide essential data about the whales' health
Eba, a rescue dog trained in orca feces scent-detection, takes point on the bow of research vessel steered by owner and killer whale researcher Dr. Deborah Giles, on Puget Sound near Bainbridge Island, Washington, on Nov. 17, 2026. Photo by Lindsey Wasson/AP (NMFS/NOAA permit #26288-01)
Over the years, the team has collected hundreds of fecal and breath samples. Those contain hormonal, bacterial, fungal, parasitic, and DNA information that is sent to the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance lab for analysis. The data is then compiled to create health profiles for individual orcas.

A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again
World
Nov 27, 2026 1:19 PM EST
BRUSSELS (AP) — After struggling to chaperone Europe's leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. "We didn't reach an agreement," he said.
Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.
READ MORE: Zelenskyy urges the U.S. to pressure Putin, calling Trump's 'my friend' remark strange
The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world's biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.
Costa said "some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts."
It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.
In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.
Costa wants a new budget agreed by end of year
In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.
Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.
"This is a negotiation process," he said. "It's normal that the member states try to defend their own national interests."
"For me, it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December," Costa said. He insisted that a new budget must be in place by Jan. 1, 2028. "In order to do this, we need to reach a final agreement by the end of this year," he said.
Elections in France and elsewhere complicate talks
French President Emmanuel Macron said elections in his country in April, which hard right figurehead Marine Le Pen is favorite to win, mean that he is not willing to negotiate further in 2027.
"I won't be politically and democratically in a position after December 31 to be able to relaunch a discussion on the budget and to conclude it," he said, as it will be "a period much too close to the presidential elections."
Spain has elections this weekend. Voters head to the polls in Italy and Poland next year.
READ MORE: Zelenskyy warns of imminent major Russian attack on Ukraine's power grid
Macron said he's willing to sign up to "a good agreement" at the next summit on Dec. 17-18. But he said Europe is making "a strategic error" if it narrows its ambitions, and that "France will not accept more cuts."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz noted that two days have been set aside for the next budget talks but that "it could be longer. I want to be home by Christmas."
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, a newcomer to EU budget haggling, said he had seen "zero results" and that a deal by "Christmas looks unlikely."
The search for extra budget money
If the leaders continue to clutch their purse strings, money will have to be found elsewhere, but not just for the bloc's traditional policies and future ambitions.
Funds are also needed to pay down debt on the 850-billion-euro ($932 billion) loan that was agreed after the last long-term budget negotiations to dig Europe out of its worst-ever recession, sparked by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Costa has proposed an EU-wide tax on digital services. It would be drawn from online advertising and money that companies make from user data, and could amount to 5 billion euros ($5.5 billion) a year.
READ MORE: EU accuses Russia of stalling Ukraine peace talks to target power plants as winter nears
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin voiced "strong opposition" to the levy. "Europe is reducing competitiveness and we feel, in principle, a digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," he said.
But European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that inside the room the tax had "gathered broad support, and I see good prospects for a solid package of new own resources."
The EU already raises its "own resources" through customs duties and value added tax, and the commission is exploring ways to find more through the carbon emissions trading system and a tobacco duty.
Solve the budget puzzle, and Ukraine's loan could fall into place
Recent budget proposals foresee a 100 billion-euro ($110 billion) envelope for Ukraine over seven years. The leaders must also decide on a new 45 billion-euro ($49.4 billion) loan to help meet Kyiv's economic and military needs next year.
A big issue is whether to deduct the interest that European countries pay on that loan from the budget envelope, or put more in to cover it. Ukraine will only reimburse the loan once Russia pays war reparation costs.
A year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of 90 billion euros ($99 billion) to cover most of Ukraine's needs
